title: VIII. The Scandalous Scene
paragraphs: Miüsov was a man of breeding and delicacy, and as he arrived at the Father Superior’s with Ivan, he couldn’t help feeling a little uneasy inside. He was ashamed that he had lost his temper. A man like him, he thought, ought to have held that despicable wretch Fyodor Pavlovitch in too much contempt to be rattled by him in Father Zossima’s cell, and so to forget himself. “The monks weren’t to blame, anyway,” he told himself on the steps. “And if they’re decent people here (the Father Superior, I hear, is a nobleman), why shouldn’t I be friendly and polite to them? I won’t argue. I’ll agree to everything. I’ll win them over with good manners, and ... and ... make it clear that I have nothing to do with that Æsop, that buffoon, that Pierrot, and was simply fooled into this business, as they were.”

He made up his mind to end his lawsuit with the monastery and give up, then and there, his claims to the timber and fishing rights. He was all the more willing because those rights had lost much of their value, and he had only the haziest notion where the woods and river in question lay.

These good intentions only grew when he walked into the Father Superior’s dining room. Strictly speaking, it wasn’t a dining room at all, because the Father Superior had just two rooms, though they were far bigger and more comfortable than Father Zossima’s. There was no great luxury in them either. The furniture was old-fashioned mahogany covered in leather, in the style of 1820. The floor wasn’t even painted, but everything was spotless, and there were lots of fine flowers in the windows. The richest thing in the room just then was, naturally, the handsomely set table. The tablecloth was clean and the tableware sparkled. There were three kinds of well-baked bread, two bottles of wine, two of excellent mead, and a big glass jug of kvas. The mead and kvas were both made at the monastery and well known throughout the district. There was no vodka. Rakitin said afterwards that there were five courses: sterlet soup with little fish pies; then boiled fish prepared in a special way; then salmon cutlets, ice pudding and compote; and last, blanc-mange. Rakitin knew all about these delicacies because he couldn’t resist peeking into the kitchen, where he already had his foot in the door. He had his foot in the door everywhere and picked up news about everything. He had a restless, envious nature. He knew very well how talented he was, and in his vanity he anxiously overestimated it. He was sure he would play some prominent role. Alyosha, who was fond of him, was grieved to see that Rakitin was dishonorable without realizing it himself. Rakitin thought just the opposite: because he wouldn’t steal money left lying on a table, he was a man of the highest integrity. Neither Alyosha nor anyone else could have talked him out of that.

Rakitin, of course, was far too minor a figure to be asked to the dinner. Of the monks, only Father Iosif, Father Païssy and one other had been invited. They were already waiting when Miüsov, Kalganov and Ivan came in. The other guest, Maximov, stood slightly apart, waiting as well. The Father Superior came forward to the middle of the room to greet his guests. He was a tall, thin but still vigorous old man, his black hair streaked with gray, his face long, grave and ascetic. He bowed to his guests without a word. This time they went up to ask his blessing. Miüsov even tried to kiss his hand, but the Father Superior pulled it back in time to avoid the kiss. Ivan and Kalganov, however, carried out the ritual wholeheartedly and in full, kissing his hand the way peasants do.

“We must humbly apologize, your reverence,” Miüsov began, with an affable simper and in a dignified, respectful tone. “Please forgive us for arriving without the gentleman you invited, Fyodor Pavlovitch. He felt he had to decline the honor of your hospitality, and with good reason. In the reverend Father Zossima’s cell he got carried away by the unfortunate quarrel with his son and said some things that were quite out of place ... indeed, quite improper ... as”—he glanced at the monks—“your reverence no doubt knows already. So, seeing that he was at fault, he felt real regret and shame, and asked me and his son Ivan Fyodorovitch to bring you his apologies and regrets. In short, he hopes and means to make amends later. He asks for your blessing and begs you to forget what happened.”
With the last word of his tirade, Miüsov was entirely pleased with himself again, and no trace was left of his earlier irritation. He loved humanity once more, fully and sincerely.
The Father Superior heard him out with dignity and, bowing his head slightly, answered:
“I truly regret that he is not here. Perhaps at our table he would have come to like us, and we him. Do sit down, gentlemen.”
He stood in front of the holy icon and began to say grace aloud. All bowed their heads respectfully, and Maximov clasped his hands before him with unusual fervor.

At this moment Fyodor Pavlovitch played his final prank. It should be said that he really had intended to go home. After his disgraceful behavior in the elder’s cell, he truly felt that he couldn’t go to dine with the Father Superior as if nothing had happened. It wasn’t that he was very ashamed of himself—perhaps quite the opposite. But he still felt it would be improper to go to dinner. And yet his creaking carriage had barely been brought round to the hotel steps, and he had barely climbed in, when he suddenly stopped. He remembered what he had said at the elder’s: “Whenever I meet people, I feel that I’m lower than all of them and that they all take me for a buffoon. So I say, let me play the buffoon, because every one of you is stupider and lower than I am.” He wanted to get his revenge on everyone for his own improper behavior. He suddenly remembered that someone had once asked him, “Why do you hate so-and-so so much?” And with his shameless impudence he had answered, “I’ll tell you. He has never done me any harm. But I played a dirty trick on him, and I’ve hated him ever since.”

As he remembered this, he smiled, quietly and spitefully, and hesitated a moment. His eyes glittered and his lips actually trembled. “Well, I’ve started, so I may as well finish,” he decided. What he mainly felt at that moment might be put like this: “There’s no restoring my reputation now. So I’ll shame them for all I’m worth. I’ll show them I don’t care what they think—and that’s that!”

He told the coachman to wait and went back to the monastery with quick steps, straight to the Father Superior’s. He had no clear idea what he would do. But he knew he could not control himself, and that the slightest push might drive him to the furthest limits of obscenity—though only obscenity, nothing criminal, nothing the law could punish him for. When it came to it, he could always hold himself back, and at times he had actually marveled at himself for that. He appeared in the Father Superior’s dining room at the moment the prayer ended and everyone was heading for the table. He stood in the doorway and surveyed the company. Then, with his long, impudent, spiteful chuckle, he looked them all boldly in the face. “They thought I’d gone, and here I am again!” he cried to the whole room.

For a moment everyone stared at him in silence, and everyone sensed at once that something revolting, grotesque, downright scandalous was about to happen. Miüsov swung from the kindest mood to the most savage. Every feeling that had calmed and died in his heart came back to life at once.
“No! I can’t stand this!” he cried. “I absolutely can’t! And ... I certainly can’t!”
The blood rushed to his head. He actually stammered, but he was beyond caring about style, and he grabbed his hat.
“What is it he can’t?” cried Fyodor Pavlovitch. “What is it he absolutely can’t and certainly can’t? Your reverence, may I come in or not? Will you take me in as your guest?”

“You are welcome with all my heart,” answered the Superior. “Gentlemen!” he added, “I dare to beg you most earnestly to put aside your quarrels and be joined in love and family harmony—with prayer to the Lord at our humble table.”
“No, no, it’s impossible!” cried Miüsov, beside himself.

“Well, if it’s impossible for Pyotr Alexandrovitch, it’s impossible for me, and I’m not staying. That’s what I came for. From now on I’m sticking with Pyotr Alexandrovitch wherever he goes. If you leave, Pyotr Alexandrovitch, I’ll leave too. If you stay, I’ll stay. Father Superior, you stung him with that talk of family harmony—he won’t admit he’s any relation of mine. That’s right, isn’t it, von Sohn? Here’s von Sohn. How do you do, von Sohn?”
“Do you mean me?” muttered Maximov, puzzled.
“Of course I mean you,” cried Fyodor Pavlovitch. “Who else? The Father Superior can’t be von Sohn.”
“But I’m not von Sohn, either. I am Maximov.”

“No, you are von Sohn. Your reverence, do you know who von Sohn was? It was a famous murder case. They killed him in a house of harlotry—I believe that’s what such places are called among you—killed him and robbed him. Old as he was, they nailed him into a box and shipped him from Petersburg to Moscow in the baggage car. While they nailed him up, the harlots sang songs and played the harp—that is, the piano. And here he is, the very same von Sohn. He’s risen from the dead, hasn’t he, von Sohn?”
“What’s happening? What is this?” voices said in the knot of monks.
“Let’s go,” Miüsov called to Kalganov.

“No, excuse me,” Fyodor Pavlovitch cut in shrilly, stepping further into the room. “Let me finish. In the cell you scolded me for behaving disrespectfully, Pyotr Alexandrovitch, just because I talked about eating gudgeon. My relation Miüsov likes his words to have _plus de noblesse que de sincérité_, but I like mine to have _plus de sincérité que de noblesse_—and damn the _noblesse_! That’s right, isn’t it, von Sohn? Father Superior, allow me. I may be a buffoon and play the buffoon, but I’m the soul of honor, and I mean to speak my mind. Yes, I’m the soul of honor, while Pyotr Alexandrovitch has nothing in him but wounded vanity. Maybe I came here to look around and speak my mind. My son Alexey is here, working out his salvation. I’m his father. His welfare matters to me, and it’s my duty to care. All the time I’ve been playing the fool, I’ve been listening and looking on the sly. And now I want to give you the last act of the show. You know how it is with us? Whatever falls stays where it fell. Once something has fallen, it has to lie there for ever. Well, not a bit of it! I want to get up again. Holy Father, I’m angry with you. Confession is a great sacrament, and I’m ready to bow down before it in reverence. But in that cell they all kneel and confess out loud. Is it right to confess out loud? The holy Fathers decreed that confession should be in secret. Only then is it a mystery, and that’s how it was in the old days. But how can I explain to him in front of everyone that I did this and that ... well, you know what I mean—sometimes it wouldn’t even be decent to speak of it—so it really is a scandal! No, Fathers, at this rate a man could be dragged along with you into the Flagellants, I suppose ... at the first chance I’ll write to the Synod, and I’ll take my son Alexey home.”

We should note here that Fyodor Pavlovitch knew just where to find the sore spot. Some time earlier, malicious rumors had gone around, and had even reached the Archbishop (not only about our monastery but about others that had elders), saying that the elders were shown too much respect, even at the expense of the Superior’s authority, that the elders misused the sacrament of confession, and so on and so on. They were absurd charges, and everywhere they had faded away on their own. But the spirit of folly that had seized Fyodor Pavlovitch, and was sweeping him along on the current of his own nerves into ever deeper shame, suggested this old slander to him. Fyodor Pavlovitch didn’t understand a word of it. He couldn’t even state it sensibly, since this time no one had knelt and confessed aloud in the elder’s cell, and so he couldn’t have seen anything of the kind. He was only speaking from a muddled memory of old slanders. But the moment his foolish tirade was out, he felt he had been talking absurd nonsense. At once he longed to prove to his audience, and above all to himself, that it had not been nonsense. And although he knew perfectly well that every word would add more absurdity, he couldn’t stop himself, and charged blindly on.
“How disgraceful!” cried Pyotr Alexandrovitch.

“Forgive me!” said the Father Superior. “It was said long ago, ‘Many have begun to speak against me and have said evil things about me. And hearing it I said to myself: it is the correction of the Lord, and He has sent it to heal my vain soul.’ And so we thank you humbly, honored guest!” And he bowed low to Fyodor Pavlovitch.

“Tut—tut—tut—sanctimonious talk and stock phrases! Old phrases and old gestures. The same old lies and ceremonial kowtowing. We know all about it. A kiss on the lips and a dagger in the heart, like in Schiller’s _Robbers_. I don’t like falsehood, Fathers. I want the truth. But the truth isn’t found in eating gudgeon, and I say so out loud! Father monks, why do you fast? Why do you expect a reward in heaven for it? For a reward like that, I’ll come and fast myself! No, saintly monk, you try being virtuous out in the world. Do some good for society, without locking yourself in a monastery at other people’s expense and without hoping for a reward up above—you’ll find that a bit harder. I can talk sense too, Father Superior. What have they got here?” He went up to the table. “Old port wine, and mead brewed by the Eliseyev Brothers. Fie, fie, Fathers! That’s a long way past gudgeon. Look at the bottles the fathers have set out, he he he! And who paid for all this? The Russian peasant, the working man, brings the farthing he earned with his horny hand, wrung from his family and the tax collector! You bleed the people, you know, holy fathers.”
“This is too disgraceful!” said Father Iosif.
Father Païssy stubbornly said nothing. Miüsov rushed out of the room, and Kalganov hurried after him.

“Well, Father, I’m going after Pyotr Alexandrovitch! I won’t be coming to see you again. Beg me on your knees, and I still won’t come. I sent you a thousand roubles, and now you’ve begun watching me. He he he! No, I’ll say no more. I’m taking revenge for my youth, for all the humiliation I went through.” In a fit of pretended feeling, he banged his fist on the table. “This monastery has played a great part in my life! It’s cost me many bitter tears. You used to turn my wife against me—the crazy one. You cursed me with bell and book. You spread tales about me everywhere. Enough, fathers! This is the age of Liberalism, the age of steamers and railways. You won’t get a thousand roubles out of me, nor a hundred, no, nor a hundred farthings!”

We should note again that the monastery had never played any great part in his life, and he had never shed a bitter tear on its account. But he was so swept up in his pretended emotion that for a moment he almost believed it himself. He was so moved that he nearly wept. But in that very instant he sensed it was time to back off.
At this malicious lie the Father Superior bowed his head, and again he spoke with great weight:
“It is written again, ‘Bear with care and gladness the dishonor that comes upon you through no act of your own. Do not be confounded, and do not hate the one who has dishonored you.’ And so will we.”

“Tut, tut, tut! Thinking it over, and all the rest of the rigmarole. You think it over, Fathers. I’m off. But I’m taking my son Alexey away from here for good, on my authority as his father. Ivan Fyodorovitch, my most dutiful son, allow me to order you to follow me. Von Sohn, what are you staying for? Come to my place in town now. It’s fun there. It’s only a short verst away. Instead of lenten oil, I’ll give you roast suckling pig and kasha. We’ll have dinner with brandy and liqueur on the side.... I’ve got cloudberry wine. Hey, von Sohn, don’t miss your chance.” He went out, shouting and waving his arms.
That was the moment when Rakitin saw him and pointed him out to Alyosha.
“Alexey!” his father shouted from a distance when he caught sight of him. “You’re coming home with me today, for good. Bring your pillow and mattress, and don’t leave a trace behind.”

Alyosha stood frozen to the spot, watching the scene in silence. Meanwhile Fyodor Pavlovitch had climbed into the carriage, and Ivan was about to get in after him, grimly silent, without even turning to say goodbye to Alyosha. But now another scene of grotesque buffoonery, almost unbelievable, put the finishing touch on the whole episode. Maximov suddenly turned up at the side of the carriage. He had come running, panting, afraid of being too late. Rakitin and Alyosha saw him run. He was in such a rush that, in his impatience, he planted his foot on the step where Ivan’s left foot still rested, and gripping the carriage, he kept trying to jump in. “I’m coming with you!” he kept shouting, with a thin, merry laugh and a look of reckless glee on his face. “Take me too.”

“Look at that!” cried Fyodor Pavlovitch, delighted. “Didn’t I tell you he was von Sohn? It’s von Sohn himself, risen from the dead. Well, how did you tear yourself away? What did you _vonsohn_ there? And how did you get out of the dinner? You must have a brass face! I have one myself, but you surprise me, brother! Jump in, jump in! Make room, Ivan. It’ll be fun. He can lie somewhere at our feet. Will you lie at our feet, von Sohn? Or sit up on the box with the coachman. Hop up on the box, von Sohn!”
But Ivan, who had already taken his seat, said nothing and punched Maximov hard in the chest, sending him flying. It was pure luck that he didn’t fall.
“Drive on!” Ivan shouted angrily to the coachman.
“Why, what are you doing? What’s the matter with you? Why did you do that?” Fyodor Pavlovitch protested.
But the carriage had already pulled away. Ivan gave no answer.
“Well, you’re quite a fellow,” Fyodor Pavlovitch said again.

After a two-minute pause, with a sidelong look at his son, he said, “It was you who cooked up this whole monastery business, wasn’t it? You pushed for it, you approved of it. So why are you angry now?”
“You’ve talked enough rubbish. Give it a rest now,” Ivan snapped sullenly.
Fyodor Pavlovitch fell silent again for two minutes.
“A drop of brandy would be nice now,” he observed, as if uttering a great truth, but Ivan made no response.
“You’ll have some too, when we get home.”
Ivan was still silent.
Fyodor Pavlovitch waited another two minutes.
“But I’ll take Alyosha away from the monastery all the same, however much it annoys you, most honored Karl von Moor.”
Ivan shrugged contemptuously, turned away, and stared at the road. They didn’t speak again all the way home.
